Baptism of Christ
BAP-tiz-uhm uhv KRYST
doctrinal phrase
From baptism (Greek baptisma, a washing, immersion) and Christ; the baptism of the Lord Jesus by John in the Jordan.

📖 Biblical Definition

The baptism of Christ is the baptism of the Lord Jesus by John in the river Jordan at the outset of His public ministry, recorded in all four Gospels and rich in doctrine. John’s was a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, and he protested that he had need to be baptized of Jesus; but the Lord answered, “Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness.” The sinless One submitted to baptism not because He had any sin to confess, but to fulfill all righteousness, to identify Himself with the people He came to save, and to consecrate Himself to His mediatorial work. At His baptism the whole Trinity was manifested: the Son standing in the water, the Spirit descending upon Him as a dove, and the Father’s voice from heaven declaring, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Thus the baptism is at once a revelation of the triune God, the public anointing of the Messiah for His office by the Spirit, and the Father’s open approval of the Son. The dictionary receives the baptism of Christ as the inauguration of His ministry and a standing witness to the Trinity, while noting that His baptism, unique to His person and office, is not the pattern for the meaning of Christian baptism, which is the believer’s confession of union with Christ in His death, burial, and resurrection.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The baptism of the sinless Christ by John in Jordan, to fulfill all righteousness and consecrate His ministry; the occasion of the Trinity’s manifestation and the Father’s approval of the Son.

expand to see more

BAPTISM OF CHRIST, the baptism of the Lord Jesus by John in the Jordan.

Submitted to not for sin but “to fulfil all righteousness.”

The public anointing of the Messiah for His ministry by the Spirit.

The occasion of the Trinity’s manifestation: Son, Spirit as a dove, and the Father’s voice.

The Father’s open approval: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

📖 Key Scripture

Mat 3:15 — "And Jesus answering said unto him, Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness. Then he suffered him."

Mat 3:16 — "And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him:"

Mat 3:17 — "And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."

Luk 3:22 — "And the Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape like a dove upon him, and a voice came from heaven, which said, Thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Trinitarian witness of the baptism is denied by anti-Trinitarians, and its sinless purpose distorted by those who make Christ a repentant sinner.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the plain Trinitarian revelation at the Jordan: the Son in the water, the Spirit descending as a dove, the Father speaking from heaven—three distinct Persons, one God, manifest in a single scene. Against every anti-Trinitarian scheme, whether the modalism that makes Father, Son, and Spirit mere masks of one Person, or the unitarianism that denies the Son’s deity, the baptism of Christ stands as a clear scriptural witness to the holy Trinity.

A second corruption misreads the purpose of the baptism, suggesting that Christ submitted because He needed cleansing, and so denying His sinlessness. The text forbids it: He came to “fulfil all righteousness,” identifying with sinners He came to save, not confessing sins of His own. He was holy, harmless, undefiled. The dictionary holds both truths—the Son’s spotless purity and His gracious identification with His people—and distinguishes His unique baptism from Christian baptism, which signifies the believer’s union with Christ crucified and risen.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The baptism marks the anointing of the Messiah and the manifestation of the triune God at the Jordan.

expand to see more

Greek baptizō — to baptize, immerse, wash; John’s baptism of repentance.

Greek dikaiosunē — righteousness; “to fulfil all righteousness.”

The dove — the visible sign of the Spirit’s descent and anointing.

The voice from heaven — the Father’s testimony to the beloved Son.

The scene reveals the three Persons of the Godhead distinctly and at once.

Usage

"The baptism of Christ is cited as a clear scriptural manifestation of the Trinity."

"“To fulfil all righteousness” is preached on Christ’s identification with His people."

"It is distinguished from Christian baptism, which signifies union with the crucified and risen Christ."
